title: The driver with the bad back
name: Omar
description: Long-distance lorry driver, twenty-eight years on the same routes. Lives on service station food and sleeps in the cab four nights a week. His wife noticed he had gone grey in the face and drove him here herself.
personality: Gruff and self-reliant. Does not like being looked at. Answers in as few words as he can manage and resents the chair. Softens considerably if you treat him as a working man rather than a patient.
symptoms: I have a gnawing burn right here under my ribs
it eases for an hour if I eat something
I have gone light-headed standing up out of the cab
I am worn out in a way sleep does not fix
I have gone off my food entirely this last week
lie_topic: the tablets you take for your back
lie: I take the odd one for my back. Nothing regular, a couple a week at most.
truth: I have been taking eight or nine a day for months. I buy them by the box at the services. It is the only way I can sit in that seat for ten hours.
cracks_when: pressed on it a second time, or asked what his wife would say about the boxes
red_herrings: blames it on service station food and bad coffee
says his back is the only thing really wrong with him
key_questions: what painkillers have you been taking
have you noticed anything odd in the toilet

canned.have you noticed anything odd in the toi: It has been black as tar for a few days. I put it down to the iron in those tablets.
canned.have you vomited anything: Once, yesterday, in the lay-by. It looked like old coffee grounds.
canned.do you drink alcohol: A few beers at the weekend when I am home. Nothing in the week, I am driving.
canned._greeting: My wife made me come. I have got a load to get to Leeds.
canned._whats_wrong: My back, mostly. The rest is service station food.
_deflect: It is what I eat. You try living off those places.
My back is the problem. Always has been.
How long is this going to take? I have got a load booked.
I have had worse and worked through it.
My wife worries. That is her job, not yours.
canned._feeling: A burn, right under the ribs. Eating shifts it for an hour.

exam.general: Grey, clammy and sitting very still. Looks older than fifty-two today.
exam.abdominal: Soft, with tenderness high in the middle. No guarding, no rebound. No organ enlargement. Rectal examination shows black tarry stool.
exam.cardiovascular: Tachycardic 112. BP 108/62 lying, 86/50 sitting up. Peripheries cool.
exam.hands: Pale palmar creases. Capillary refill 3 seconds. No clubbing.

level_card: Fifty-two, grey in the face, and worried about a load booked for Leeds.
He has a burn under his ribs that eating settles.
Ask what he buys at the services, and how many.
reveal_note: A couple a week was eight or nine a day, bought by the box, for months.
opening_line: My wife made me come. I have got a load to get to Leeds.

presentation.complaint: Burning pain under the ribs and light-headedness
presentation.duration: The burn has been months. The dizziness is this week
presentation.triage_note: Brought by wife. Grey, clammy, marked postural drop. Reports black motions for several days.

past_medical: My back. Twenty years of it
Nothing else worth troubling you with
social: I drive lorries, long distance, twenty-eight years
I sleep in the cab four nights a week
I smoked until I was forty
A few beers at the weekend when I am home
family: My father died of his heart at sixty
My mother is still going strong

harmful_treatments.nsaid: The tablets are the cause. Another one is the single worst thing you could give him.
harmful_treatments.aspirin_loading: He is actively bleeding. Loading him with an antiplatelet makes it worse.

management_points: Two large-bore cannulae, bloods including a cross-match, and fluid or blood for shock
Calculate a risk score (Blatchford on admission) rather than eyeballing him
Stop the culprit: the NSAIDs are the cause, not a detail of the history
Proton pump inhibitor and urgent endoscopy, within 24 hours and sooner if unstable
Transfuse to a restrictive target, around 70-80 g/L, unless he is exsanguinating
A postural drop of that size is a large loss already; do not be reassured by a lying pressure
Check coagulation and reverse anticoagulation if present

teaching.summary: A 52-year-old driver taking eight or nine ibuprofen a day for his back, now with melaena, coffee-ground vomit and a 22-point postural drop. He described it as a couple a week.
pearls: Ask how many, not whether. 'The odd one' is never the odd one.
A postural drop is the cheapest measure of blood loss you have.
Black tarry stool is a diagnosis, not a curiosity.
Restrictive transfusion saves lives; over-transfusion does not.
The patient who wants to leave for work is often the sickest in the department.

key_question_reasons: Eight or nine a day, bought by the box, for months. High-dose NSAIDs on an empty stomach for ten-hour shifts is the cause, and he calls it 'a couple a week'.
Black tarry stool is digested blood. It is the finding that turns a sore stomach into an emergency.
Coffee-ground vomit is the same blood from the other end, and tells you the bleed is upper gastrointestinal.
Alcohol on top of NSAIDs multiplies the risk, and changes what you watch for after admission.
